1.why: Verify-token compares the submitted code only to the current session’s resetTokenHash and rejects mismatches, so the code must belong to that session’s recovery flow.

2.why: Reset hashes live per session; another session does not hold the same resetTokenHash, so the same code does not work for a different user/session.

3.why: Password reset only updates the current session object and never invalidates or enumerates other sessions, so any prior sessions would keep working.

4.why: Bun.serve is configured with TLS certificates and HSTS, and non-HTTPS X-Forwarded-Proto is rejected, though the exact TLS version is not pinned in code.

5.why: Reset tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes and passwords via bcrypt; in-memory session fields are not further encrypted at rest.

6.why: There is no real email sender; the simulated delivery returns the raw token in the API/UI log, while account-existence messaging stays generic.

7.why: Inputs are allowlisted (validAccountInput/validToken/validPassword) and client output uses textContent, not raw HTML interpolation.

8.why: resetPath is a same-origin relative /reset URL built only from a server-generated token; no user-controlled external redirects exist.

9.why: No email HTML templates render user input; simulated delivery is plain text via textContent/logging only.

10.why: Error JSON is generic, but the on-page activity log and recovery API response deliberately expose recovery tokens and the MFA code.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed in session state, but the MFA secret is the hardcoded constant MFA_CODE = "482915" in source.

12.why: No default username/password login exists; only the simulated fixed MFA code is constant, not general default credentials.

13.why: Both reset-token and MFA verification increment failure counters and set resetBlockedUntil/mfaBlockedUntil after five bad attempts.

14.why: /api/recovery returns the same eligible-wording success path for any well-formed account string and does not disclose whether the account exists.

15.why: Recovery tokens come from crypto.getRandomValues (32 bytes, base64url), are hashed and bound to the issuing session, and expire/single-use flags apply.
